questions.q: Across the biological membrane in the absorption diagram, which group of mechanisms is bracketed as 'ATP not required'?
opts: Filtration, simple/passive diffusion and facilitated diffusion
questions.exp: The brace labelled 'ATP not required' covers filtration, simple (passive) diffusion and facilitated diffusion; only active transport needs ATP. (Book p2)

questions.q: The absorption mechanism illustrated in the diagram with the example 'insulin (subcutaneous)' is:
questions.exp: Filtration is passage of drug through pores of the biological membrane; the example given is insulin administered subcutaneously. (Book p2)

questions.q: The commonest (m/c) mechanism of drug absorption shown in the diagram is:
questions.exp: Simple/passive diffusion is marked m/c; it occurs along the concentration gradient and requires no ATP. (Book p2)

questions.q: Which mechanism of absorption is carrier-mediated but does NOT require ATP?
questions.exp: Facilitated diffusion uses a carrier (e.g. GLUT receptors) but still follows the concentration gradient and needs no ATP, so it lies on the 'ATP not required' side of the diagram. (Book p2)

questions.q: In the absorption diagram, the example given for facilitated diffusion is:
questions.exp: GLUT receptors illustrate facilitated diffusion, and GLUT absorption is stated to be based on the concentration gradient. (Book p2)

questions.q: The diagram gives which example for ATP-requiring active transport?
questions.exp: Active transport (ATP required) is illustrated by SGLT receptors, with SGLT-1 on small intestine and SGLT-2 on renal tubules. (Book p2)

questions.q: SGLT-1 receptors are located on the:
questions.exp: SGLT-1 is on the small intestine; SGLT-2 is on renal tubules. (Book p2)

questions.q: SGLT-2 receptors are located on the:
questions.exp: SGLT-2 is on renal tubules, whereas SGLT-1 is on the small intestine - the pair is given as the example of active transport. (Book p2)

questions.q: 'Carrier mediated transport' in the absorption diagram includes:
opts: Filtration, simple diffusion and facilitated diffusion
questions.exp: The carrier-mediated bracket spans facilitated diffusion and active transport; filtration and simple/passive diffusion need no carrier. (Book p2)

questions.q: Which mechanism of absorption is independent of the concentration gradient?
questions.exp: Active transport is labelled 'independent of conc. gradient' and requires ATP; the other three proceed along the concentration gradient. (Book p2)

questions.q: Which statement about simple/passive diffusion is correct?
opts: It occurs along the concentration gradient without ATP
It occurs against the concentration gradient with ATP
It requires a carrier but no ATP
questions.exp: Simple/passive diffusion (the m/c mechanism) moves drug along the concentration gradient without a carrier and without ATP. (Book p2)

questions.q: In the diagram of the biological membrane, filtration of a drug occurs through:
questions.exp: Filtration is drawn as drug crossing the membrane through pores, with subcutaneous insulin as the example. (Book p2)

questions.q: Which mechanism-example pair is correctly matched in the absorption diagram?
questions.exp: Filtration is matched to subcutaneous insulin, facilitated diffusion to GLUT receptors, and active transport to SGLT receptors (SGLT-1 gut, SGLT-2 renal tubule). (Book p2)

questions.q: The P-glycoprotein (pgp) pump is also known as:
questions.exp: The heading reads 'Active transport: P-glycoprotein pump (pgp)/MDR1 pump'. (Book p2)

questions.q: P-glycoprotein (MDR1) is the most common type of:
questions.exp: A note under the heading states pgp/MDR1 is the m/c type of ABC (ATP-binding cassette) pump - a primary active transporter. (Book p2)

questions.q: Efflux by the P-glycoprotein pump on the intestinal epithelial cell moves drug:
opts: From within the cell back into the intestinal lumen
From the intestinal lumen into the blood vessel lumen
From blood into the intestinal lumen
From the intestinal lumen into the lymphatics
questions.exp: The pgp on the epithelial cell pumps absorbed drug back out into the intestinal lumen - drug efflux - opposite to absorption. (Book p3)

questions.q: Most drugs cross the gut epithelium along the concentration gradient, but some are effluxed back so that drug is excreted before reaching the systemic circulation. This is called:
questions.exp: The diagram writes 'Some drugs efflux: First pass metabolism - drug excreted before reaching systemic circulation'. (Book p3)

questions.q: Which drug's dosage is calculated based on the amount being lost due to drug efflux?
questions.exp: The book's stated significance of P-gp efflux: digoxin dosage is calculated based on the amount being lost due to drug efflux. (Book p3)

questions.q: Loperamide, an opioid used in the treatment of diarrhoea, is useful as an antidiarrhoeal because it acts on the:
questions.exp: Loperamide is an opioid that acts on the GIT, which is why it controls diarrhoea without central opioid effects. (Book p3)

questions.q: Loperamide cannot cross the blood brain barrier because:
opts: MDR1 pumps are present in the BBB
It has no affinity for opioid receptors
questions.exp: MDR1 pumps are present in the BBB and efflux loperamide, so the opioid cannot reach the CNS; this is exactly why it can be used for diarrhoea. (Book p3)

questions.q: Apart from efflux by MDR1 pumps, the other cause stated for drugs not crossing the BBB is:
questions.exp: A note reads 'Another cause of drugs not crossing BBB - water solubility'; both efflux pumps and water solubility limit CNS entry. (Book p3)

questions.q: Certain drugs cannot cross from maternal circulation to fetal circulation because of MDR1 pumps present in the:
questions.exp: The book states that certain drugs cannot cross from maternal to fetal circulation due to the presence of MDR1 pumps in the placenta. (Book p3)

questions.q: Bile acid excretion occurs due to the presence of MDR1 pumps on:
questions.exp: Bile acid excretion is attributed to the presence of MDR1 pumps on hepatocytes. (Book p3)

questions.q: Which site-MDR1 pump pair is correctly matched?
opts: Placenta - prevents certain drugs crossing from mother to fetus
Hepatocytes - prevent drug crossing into bile
BBB - water-soluble drugs are pumped back into blood
Intestinal epithelial cell - pumps drug into the systemic circulation
questions.exp: MDR1 pumps in the placenta stop certain drugs reaching the fetus; on hepatocytes they mediate bile acid excretion; in the BBB they eject drugs like loperamide; in the gut epithelium they efflux drug back into the lumen. (Book p3)

questions.q: In bacteria and tumour cells, drug resistance develops by which sequence?
opts: Cell develops Pgp pump - drug efflux - resistance
Cell develops pores - drug influx - resistance
Cell develops SGLT receptor - active uptake - resistance
Cell develops GLUT receptor - facilitated diffusion - resistance
questions.exp: The flowchart reads: Cell - develops - Pgp pump - drug efflux - resistance. (Book p3)

questions.q: The mechanism by which a Pgp-pump-expressing tumour cell resists chemotherapy is:
opts: The pump actively effluxes the drug out of the cell, lowering the intracellular drug concentration
The pump metabolises the drug inside the cell
The cell stops taking up the drug through GLUT receptors
The cell develops pores that leak the drug out
questions.exp: The Pgp pump drives drug efflux, so less drug stays inside the cell - the same efflux mechanism produces resistance in bacteria and tumour cells. (Book p3)

questions.q: According to the pharmacological significance flowchart, P-gp inducers cause:
opts: Increase in the number of pumps, producing drug failure
Decrease in the number of pumps, producing drug toxicity
Increase in the number of pumps, producing drug toxicity
Decrease in the number of pumps, producing drug failure
questions.exp: Inducers increase the number of pumps, and this causes drug failure because more drug is effluxed out. (Book p4)

questions.q: P-gp inducers are considered analogous to:
questions.exp: The flowchart marks P-gp inducers as 'approximately equal to enzyme inducers' - the same drugs that induce microsomal enzymes also induce the efflux pump. (Book p4)

questions.q: Which group lists only P-gp inducers?
questions.exp: The inducer list is rifampicin, phenytoin and phenobarbital - the classic enzyme inducers. (Book p4)

questions.q: Which group lists only P-gp substrates (drugs that undergo efflux by the pump)?
questions.exp: The substrate column lists loperamide, cyclosporine and digoxin as drugs that undergo efflux by the pump. (Book p4)

questions.q: Which group lists only P-gp inhibitors?
questions.exp: The inhibitor list is verapamil, amiodarone, quinidine, cyclosporine, itraconazole, neratinib and erythromycin/clarithromycin. (Book p4)

questions.q: P-gp inhibitors decrease the number of pumps and therefore cause:
questions.exp: The flowchart states inhibitors decrease the number of pumps, which causes drug toxicity because less drug is effluxed and more stays in the body. (Book p4)

questions.q: Which drug appears in BOTH the substrate and the inhibitor lists of P-gp?
questions.exp: Cyclosporine is listed both as a substrate (undergoes efflux) and as a P-gp inhibitor, so it can raise the levels of co-administered P-gp substrates. (Book p4)

questions.q: Which macrolide antibiotics are listed as P-gp inhibitors?
questions.exp: Erythromycin/clarithromycin are given among the P-gp inhibitors. (Book p4)

questions.q: Neratinib is listed in the flowchart as a P-gp:
questions.exp: Neratinib appears in the inhibitor column, along with verapamil, amiodarone, quinidine, cyclosporine, itraconazole and erythromycin/clarithromycin. (Book p4)

questions.q: As per the table of effects of blockade, rifampicin blocking P-gp results in:
questions.exp: The table pairs rifampicin (drug blocking Pgp) with digoxin failure - loss of digoxin effect. (Book p4)

questions.q: Which drug blocking P-gp causes digoxin toxicity?
questions.exp: The table pairs clarithromycin with digoxin toxicity, because blocking the efflux pump raises digoxin levels. (Book p4)

questions.q: Blockade of P-gp by cyclosporine is associated with:
questions.exp: The table lists cyclosporine as a P-gp blocker producing cholestatic jaundice. (Book p4)

questions.q: Which drug blocking P-gp is used in the reversal of drug resistance in cancer and bacteria?
questions.exp: The table pairs verapamil with 'used in reversal of drug resistance (cancer, bacteria)'. (Book p4)

questions.q: Quinidine blocks P-gp and thereby causes:
questions.exp: The table pairs quinidine blockade of P-gp with loperamide-induced central side effects. (Book p4)

questions.q: A patient on loperamide develops central opioid side effects after quinidine is added. The best explanation is:
opts: Quinidine inhibits P-gp, so loperamide is no longer effluxed at the BBB and enters the CNS
Quinidine induces P-gp, increasing loperamide efflux into the brain
Quinidine displaces loperamide from plasma proteins
Quinidine increases gastric emptying of loperamide
questions.exp: Normally MDR1 pumps in the BBB keep loperamide out of the CNS; quinidine blocks P-gp, loperamide crosses into the brain and produces central side effects. (Book p4)

questions.q: In the passive diffusion diagram, the ovals drawn within the lipid bilayer are labelled:
questions.exp: Both membrane ovals are labelled 'Proteins charged' - the charged proteins that repel charged drug molecules. (Book p4)

questions.q: A polar/ionised/charged drug reaching the intestinal lumen is:
opts: Repelled and not absorbed, being water soluble and excreted
Absorbed because it is lipid soluble
questions.exp: Polar/ionised/charged drug is repelled by the charged proteins of the lipid membrane, is not absorbed (lipid insoluble/water soluble) and is excreted. (Book p4)

questions.q: Which drug characteristics favour passage by passive diffusion?
questions.exp: Non-polar/unionised/neutral drug is lipid soluble and is therefore absorbed by passive diffusion. (Book p4)

questions.q: From the passive diffusion figure, absorption of a drug across a lipid membrane is determined mainly by:
opts: Lipid solubility of the non-ionised form
Water solubility of the ionised form
Number of P-gp pumps in the membrane
questions.exp: The figure contrasts non-polar/unionised/neutral (lipid soluble - absorbed) with polar/ionised/charged (water soluble - repelled and excreted), so lipid solubility governs passive diffusion. (Book p4)

questions.q: Which statement best summarises the passive diffusion figure?
opts: Non-polar unionised drug is absorbed, while polar ionised drug is repelled by charged membrane proteins and excreted
Polar and non-polar drugs are absorbed equally
Polar drugs are absorbed by carriers and non-polar drugs by pores
Only charged membrane proteins are absorbed
questions.exp: The figure shows non-polar/unionised/neutral drug crossing to the blood vessel lumen (absorbed, lipid soluble), while polar/ionised/charged drug is repelled and is not absorbed (water soluble, excreted). (Book p4)

units.title: Absorption: Four Transport Mechanisms
units.guide: Drugs cross the biological membrane by four routes: filtration through pores (subcutaneous insulin), simple/passive diffusion (the commonest, along the concentration gradient), facilitated diffusion via carriers such as GLUT receptors, and ATP-dependent active transport via SGLT receptors - SGLT-1 in the small intestine and SGLT-2 in renal tubules. Filtration, simple diffusion and facilitated diffusion need no ATP; only active transport is independent of the concentration gradient, and the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) pump, the commonest ABC pump, is the prototype efflux transporter.

units.title: P-gp in Gut and Liver: Efflux and First Pass
units.guide: In the small intestine and liver the P-glycoprotein pump sits on the epithelial cell and pushes absorbed drug back into the lumen - efflux. Some drugs are thereby excreted before ever reaching the systemic circulation, which is why this is labelled first pass metabolism, and digoxin dosage is calculated from the amount lost this way.

units.title: Crossing Barriers: BBB, Placenta, Hepatocytes
units.guide: MDR1 pumps are placed at every barrier of the body. Loperamide, an opioid acting on the GIT for diarrhoea, cannot enter the brain because BBB MDR1 pumps eject it - and water solubility is another reason drugs fail to cross the BBB. Placental MDR1 pumps keep certain drugs away from the fetus, and hepatocyte MDR1 pumps mediate bile acid excretion.

units.title: P-gp and Drug Resistance
units.guide: A bacterial or tumour cell that develops a Pgp pump effluxes the drug out of the cell, lowering the intracellular concentration, and so becomes resistant. This single flowchart explains multidrug resistance in infections and in cancer chemotherapy.

units.title: P-gp Substrates, Inducers and Inhibitors
units.guide: Three groups matter clinically: substrates that are effluxed (loperamide, cyclosporine, digoxin), inducers that increase the number of pumps and cause drug failure - rifampicin, phenytoin, phenobarbital, mirroring enzyme inducers - and inhibitors that decrease the number of pumps and cause drug toxicity (verapamil, amiodarone, quinidine, cyclosporine, itraconazole, neratinib, erythromycin/clarithromycin). Cyclosporine appears in both the substrate and the inhibitor lists.

units.title: Effects of P-gp Blockade
units.guide: The blockade table gives drug-specific outcomes: rifampicin leads to digoxin failure, clarithromycin to digoxin toxicity, cyclosporine to cholestatic jaundice, verapamil is used to reverse drug resistance in cancer and bacteria, and quinidine unmasks loperamide-induced central side effects by opening the BBB to this normally excluded opioid.

units.title: Passive Diffusion and Lipid Solubility
units.guide: The passive diffusion figure carries charged proteins within the lipid bilayer. Polar, ionised or charged drug is repelled, remains lipid insoluble/water soluble and is excreted, whereas a non-polar, unionised, neutral drug is lipid soluble and is absorbed. Lipid solubility of the unionised fraction is therefore the key determinant of passive diffusion.
